summary: Isopropyl alcohol (isopropanol, 2-propanol) is an aliphatic alcohol used as a topical antiseptic and surface disinfectant, classically as 70% 'rubbing alcohol'. It rapidly denatures microbial proteins and disrupts membranes, killing bacteria, many viruses and fungi. It is used to disinfect intact skin before injections or procedures and to clean minor cuts and surfaces. It is for EXTERNAL use only - it is highly flammable, and ingestion is toxic (CNS depression, gastritis).
indications: Antiseptic preparation of intact skin before injection, venepuncture or minor procedures
First-aid antiseptic to help decrease germs on minor cuts and scrapes (per OTC monograph)

dosage.t: Apply and allow to air-dry before procedure
dosage.n: Single use; let dry fully (also reduces flammability before any cautery)

dosage.d: Apply to the affected area 1-3 times daily
dosage.n: Do not apply over large body areas or use on deep/serious wounds

admin: EXTERNAL USE ONLY - never swallow; ingestion is toxic
Apply to intact skin and allow to air-dry, especially before any electrocautery or diathermy (pooled alcohol can ignite)
Avoid contact with eyes, mucous membranes and large or broken skin areas
Use in a well-ventilated area; vapour is irritating and flammable
Keep away from flames, sparks and heat sources; store securely away from children
moa: Isopropyl alcohol acts by denaturing and coagulating microbial proteins and dissolving lipid membranes, causing rapid cell lysis and death. Antimicrobial activity is greatest around 60-90% concentration (water is required to facilitate protein denaturation), which is why 70% is the typical antiseptic strength. It is bactericidal, tuberculocidal, fungicidal and active against many enveloped viruses, but is not reliably sporicidal.

absolute: Application to or near the eyes
relative: Application to large open wounds, deep/puncture wounds or burns
Use near naked flames, cautery or diathermy before the skin is dry
Neonates/premature infants (risk of chemical burns and absorption on occluded/fragile skin)
monitor: Local skin irritation, dryness or dermatitis
Adequate drying before any ignition source
Signs of toxicity if accidental ingestion/excess inhalation

preg: Topical use is considered acceptable; systemic absorption through intact skin is negligible. Avoid ingestion and excessive inhalation of vapour.
lact: Topical use is compatible with breastfeeding; avoid applying to the nipple/areola or wipe off before feeding to prevent infant ingestion.
renal: Not applicable to normal topical use. In significant systemic exposure/ingestion, supportive care; isopropanol and its metabolite acetone can be removed by haemodialysis in severe poisoning.
hepatic: Not applicable to topical use. If absorbed/ingested, isopropanol is metabolised by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase to acetone (no acid metabolite, so it causes ketosis without significant metabolic acidosis).

minor: Other topical agents on the same site may be affected by alcohol's drying/solvent action
interactions.alcohol: Topical product; not for drinking. Ingestion together with ethanol or accidental misuse increases CNS depression
interactions.diagnostics: Skin antisepsis with alcohol is standard before venepuncture; allow to dry to avoid haemolysis/stinging. Isopropanol ingestion raises serum osmolar gap and produces ketonaemia/ketonuria without acidosis

common: Skin dryness, irritation or transient stinging on application
serious: Chemical burns with prolonged occlusive contact (notably in neonates/infants)
Flammability - flash burns if ignited before drying
emergency: Ingestion: CNS depression, coma, respiratory depression, haemorrhagic gastritis, hypotension

monitoring: Complete drying before use of cautery/diathermy
For suspected ingestion: level of consciousness, osmolar gap, serum acetone/isopropanol, glucose and haemodynamics
counsel: For external use only - never drink it; swallowing can be poisonous
It is highly flammable - keep away from flames, cigarettes and heat, and let it dry before any procedure using cautery
Avoid the eyes and inside of the nose/mouth; do not use on large open wounds or burns
May dry the skin with repeated use
Store out of reach of children; seek emergency help and contact poison control if swallowed
pk: Rapid antimicrobial action within seconds of contact with skin/surface
Not applicable for topical use; negligible systemic absorption through intact skin
If absorbed/ingested, isopropanol half-life roughly 3-7 hours (metabolised to acetone, which is longer-lived)
Acts only while present/wet on the surface; evaporates quickly
Store in a cool place below 25 C in a tightly closed container, away from flames/ignition; keep out of reach of children
pearls: Topical antiseptic covered by the FDA OTC antiseptic monograph for EXTERNAL use; data from FDA OTC monograph, DailyMed/product labelling and pharmacopoeial sources
70% is the optimal antiseptic strength - some water is needed for protein denaturation; higher concentrations evaporate too fast and are less effective
Highly flammable: must air-dry before electrocautery/diathermy to avoid surgical fires

Ingestion is toxic - causes CNS depression and gastritis, with ketosis/ketonuria and a raised osmolar gap but, unlike methanol/ethylene glycol, no major metabolic acidosis; fomepizole is generally NOT indicated, management is supportive +/- dialysis
Not reliably sporicidal; use a sterilant for spores (e.g. C. difficile, Bacillus)
missed: Not applicable - used as needed for skin antisepsis/disinfection rather than on a fixed dosing schedule; simply apply when antisepsis is required.
overdose: Overdose results from ingestion or excessive inhalation, not normal topical use. Ingestion causes CNS depression (drowsiness, ataxia, coma), respiratory depression, hypotension, haemorrhagic gastritis with vomiting/abdominal pain, ketonaemia and a raised osmolar gap without significant acidosis. Management is supportive (airway, breathing, circulation, fluids, glucose); haemodialysis is effective in severe poisoning. Contact a poison control centre urgently.
